messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Samir is a 64-year-old divorced Middle Eastern man who has served as a city councilman for the past decade. He came to therapy at the urging of his chief of staff after several colleagues noticed he had become increasingly withdrawn and irritable during public engagements. The trauma that underpins his current difficulties occurred nearly twenty years ago, when Samir worked as a relief coordinator in a conflict-ravaged region. During a ceasefire negotiation, a roadside bomb detonated near his convoy; he was not physically injured, but for hours he lay pinned beneath the wreckage, inhaling the acrid smell of burning metal and flesh while listening to the unnerving silence that followed the blast—a quiet he has never been able to shake.

In the years since, Samir entered politics, believing that public service would give him purpose. Instead, the work has become a labyrinth of triggers. When a stranger approaches him at a town hall with a question about veteran affairs, Samir’s mind is instantly flooded with fragmented, terror-soaked images: the twisted jeep, the blood on his hands, the overwhelming helplessness. That memory often comes in disconnected pieces, so vivid that he feels the same raw terror he felt at the time, and he has to stop whatever he is doing, overcome by emotion. To manage this, he has learned to control his outward reactions rigidly—he forces a neutral expression, changes the subject, or excuses himself to his office where he immerses himself in paperwork. The burnt smell from a nearby restaurant’s grill can send him reeling; he now avoids that block altogether, or on days he cannot, he throws himself into back-to-back meetings to keep his mind occupied.

The memory itself feeds an ever-present sense of threat. After a flashback, Samir finds himself scanning every corner of the room during a committee hearing, checking that the doors and windows are locked, even though he knows rationally that his office is secure. The unusual silence that falls in a hallway between conversations makes him freeze, certain that something terrible is about to happen. On days when that sense of threat was highest, the memory would surface unbidden—a vivid flash of the wreckage—as if his mind was trying to stay ahead of the danger by reviewing it beforehand. That anxious vigilance, in turn, drives him to redouble his maladaptive efforts: he tries to control his emotions more tightly, uses distraction—turning on talk radio at home—and overworks to the point of exhaustion. Yet these strategies backfire. His constant overworking leaves him depleted and more vulnerable to intrusive memories, which then return with greater frequency and fragmentation. His rigid emotion control also prevents him from processing the trauma, so the memories stay raw, and the threat never dissipates.

As the cycle tightened, Samir’s sensitivity to triggers grew. Every military-themed news segment now feels like a direct assault; he changes the channel immediately. A stranger’s casual question during a meet-and-greet can derail his entire afternoon. The memory itself makes him more attuned to any burnt odor in the environment, and he now checks the kitchen exhaust in his home repeatedly. His avoidance has cost him: he has turned down several speaking invitations at veterans’ events, and his staff has noticed he often seems distant during conversations. His divorce years ago had already left him isolated; now his world has shrunk further.

What finally brought Samir to seek help was a public incident: at a memorial service, the smell of incense (which he associates with the burnt aftermath) triggered a full emotional shutdown. He froze, could not speak, and had to be escorted out. His chief of staff insisted he see a specialist. Sitting in the clinic, Samir is afraid that seeking therapy means admitting weakness, but he is even more afraid that the fragments of memory will eventually shatter his career. He hopes, quietly, that perhaps describing the disconnected pieces out loud might make them fit together—and that the silence he dreads might one day become just silence again.
